# Where am I? Large Language Models Wandering between Semantics and Structures in Long Contexts

Seonmin Koo $^{1*}$ , Jinsung Kim $^{1*}$ , YoungJoon Jang $^{1}$ , Chanjun Park $^{2\dagger}$ , Heuiseok Lim $^{1\dagger}$

$^{1}$ Department of Computer science and Engineering, Korea University

$^{2}$ Upstage AI

{fhdahd,jin62304,limhseok}@korea.ac.kr

yjoonjang34@gmail.com

chanjun.park@upstage.ai

# Abstract

As the utilization of Large Language Models (LLMs) becomes more widespread, there is a growing demand for their ability to handle more complex and longer external knowledge across various use cases. Most existing evaluations of the open-ended question answering (ODQA) task, which necessitates the use of external knowledge, focus solely on whether the model provides the correct answer. However, even when LLMs answer correctly, they often fail to provide an obvious source for their responses. Therefore, it is necessary to jointly evaluate and verify the correctness of the answers and the appropriateness of grounded evidence in complex external contexts. To address this issue, we examine the phenomenon of discrepancies in abilities across two distinct tasks—QA and evidence selection—when performed simultaneously, from the perspective of task alignment. To verify LLMs' task alignment, we introduce a verification framework and resources considering both semantic relevancy and structural diversity of the given long context knowledge. Through extensive experiments and detailed analysis, we provide insights into the task misalignment between QA and evidence selection. Our code and resources can be found at https://github.com/seonminkoo/WAI.

# 1 Introduction

Open-domain question answering (ODQA) task aims to generate accurate answers for a wide range of contexts and queries (Chen et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019). In the ODQA task, large language models (LLMs) should be capable of leveraging fluent generative abilities and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based capabilities to effectively utilize more complicated and longer external knowledge from the real world.

One of the challenges in leveraging diverse real-world knowledge is that knowledge contexts may not contain only helpful information for generation (Baek et al., 2023). In other words, unrelated or fascinating but partially relevant information that may confuse the model can be spread across various locations within the knowledge context (Ji et al., 2023; Bang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023). This can lead LLMs to generate hallucinated content that contradicts reality or fail to clearly present the evidence source for their responses, as illustrated in Figure 1. In particular, this phenomenon becomes more severe as the knowledge context becomes longer (Huang et al., 2023).

Despite these challenges, conventional QA research primarily evaluates whether model outputs

are included in the gold answer using metrics such as Exact Match (EM) score, thus often not focusing on the correctness of the sources underlying the generated responses (Chen et al., 2017; Lewis et al., 2020; Izacard and Grave, 2020). Recent studies on LLMs' evidence selection ability have explored various approaches, including modeling and prompting (Jo et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Kong et al., 2023). However, these studies have typically treated QA and evidence source selection as separate tasks, relatively overlooking the discrepancy in the LLMs' task alignment capabilities.

Bridging this discrepancy is crucial for ensuring the explainability of LLMs' outputs and enhancing end-user reliability (Nakano et al., 2021; Menick et al., 2022; Ras et al., 2022). Therefore, when LLMs handle extensive external knowledge, it is essential to sufficiently verify not only the accuracy of responses but also the appropriateness of the corresponding evidence selected by models.

To address these issues, we conduct an integrated and systematic study on the alignment between answer correctness and grounding appropriaten

dge, it is essential to sufficiently verify not only the accuracy of responses but also the appropriateness of the corresponding evidence selected by models.

To address these issues, we conduct an integrated and systematic study on the alignment between answer correctness and grounding appropriateness, which have traditionally been studied separately, in challenging long context settings. We explore task alignment by simultaneously performing two distinct tasks—QA and evidence selection, utilizing the same features.

For systematic validation, we conduct an empirical study on LLMs' alignment capabilities, considering both the semantic relevancy and structural diversity of the long context knowledge they utilize. Specifically, we construct semantically diverse surrounding input contexts by retrieving relevant and irrelevant information from multiple documents using the RAG approach. Additionally, we investigate the LLMs' behavior in detail by structurally diversifying the position of ground-truth evidence within complex contexts.

From a task alignment perspective, we provide insights into the discrepancy between LLMs' capabilities in QA and evidence selection through extensive experiments and detailed analysis. Furthermore, we conduct additional experiments and analyses based on context lengths and prompting strategies.

Our contributions are threefold: i) We introduce a framework and resource construction method for validating task misalignment occurring in real-world long context-based generation scenarios. ii) To achieve systematic validation, we devise the con

cepts of semantic relevancy and structural diversity, effectively investigating LLMs' task alignment capabilities and achieving enhanced explainability. iii) Through extensive experiments and analysis, we provide various insights on the LLMs' behavior in QA and evidence selection tasks when generating based on long contexts.

# 2 Related Works

# 2.1 Long context LLMs

To understand how LLMs handle long context inputs, (Li et al., 2024a; Levy et al., 2024) proposed new datasets and discovered that LLMs exhibit notable degradation in reasoning performance at much shorter input lengths than their technical maximum. Similarly, Liu et al. (2023) demonstrated the "lost-in-the-middle" phenomenon, where LLMs show lower accuracy when evidence for a query is located in the middle of a long context input. (Junqing et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024) proposed methodologies to mitigate these issues.

To evaluate the attributions of LLM-generated text, ZeroScrolls (Shaham et al., 2023), Long-Bench (Bai et al., 2023), Cab (Zhang et al., 2023), LooGLE (Li et al., 2023), and ELITR-Bench (Thonet et al., 2024) proposed to evaluation method of LLMs on long context inputs. Additionally, L-Eval (An et al., 2023) constructed datasets and investigated the effectiveness of evaluation metrics for standardized assessment.

# 2.2 LLMs with Attribution Retrieval/Generation

To mitigate hallucination in LLMs, sever

proposed to evaluation method of LLMs on long context inputs. Additionally, L-Eval (An et al., 2023) constructed datasets and investigated the effectiveness of evaluation metrics for standardized assessment.

# 2.2 LLMs with Attribution Retrieval/Generation

To mitigate hallucination in LLMs, several methodologies have been developed to generate or retrieve attributions along with sentence generation (Menick et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2023; Jain et al., 2023; Huo et al., 2023). These approaches help ensure that the responses generated by LLMs are based on reliable sources. In the retrieve-and-read paradigm, a retrieval for relevant documents within a corpus, and the language model reorders them to extract an answer (Chen et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2021). Generative retrieval has emerged as an alternative to the traditional retrieve-and-read pipeline, integrating search and generation into a single process. This approach controls the generation process by ensuring that the LLM's responses include keywords or content from the retrieved information (De Cao et al., 2020; Metzler et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024b; Sun et al., 2024).

# 3 Experimental Setup

In this section, we describe the process of constructing resources to verify the alignment between answer correctness and appropriateness of evidence selection in LLMs' responses within long-context scenarios. Additionally, we explain the models and evaluation metrics adopted for the tasks.

# 3.1 Datasets

Inspired by previous studies that validate the capabilities of existing LLMs (Chen et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2023), we experiment with the task alignment of LLMs in long contexts through QA and evidence selection tasks. For our experiment, we utilize the NQ dataset (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019), which is constructed based on Wikipedia that serves as a realistic world knowledge pool similar to a commercial search engine. This dataset includes questions formulated by users of search engines and answers manually extracted from Wikipedia. NQ dataset contains questions of formats such as 'who', 'when', and 'how many'. Detailed statistics of the dataset can be found in Appendix A.1.

To set up the challenging long-context-based tasks, we extract contexts exceeding 16k from various Wikipedia sources. For the diverse types of questions and context included, the model is expected to provide both the answer and the evidence paragraph.

# 3.2 Surrounding Context Construction

LLMs should be able to effectively utilize various external knowledge sources provided through methods such as RAG. However, in the real world, knowledge context may not contain information only beneficial for task performance, and attractive distractors could be spread across various sources (Ji et al., 2023; Bang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023). Therefore, considering these real-world challenges, we construct the surrounding contexts as illustrated in the upper part of Figure 2, considering both semantic relevancy ( $\S$ 3.2.1) and structural diversity( $\S$ 3.2.2).

# 3.2.1 Semantic Relevancy-aware Curation

Unrelated Information Unrelated information refers to contents with low relevance to the query. Most existing research extracts unrelated information by randomly selecting documents from the search pool (Yoran et al., 2023; Cuonasu et al., 2024). However, the random sampling method may include paragraphs related to the query. To prevent this, we apply low-rank retrieval. Specifically, we calculate the similarity between the query and the documents stored in Pinecone, then select the document with the lowest relevance.

Subsequently, we build an unrelated context by sequentially adding paragraphs that have low cosine similarity with the query from the selected unrelated documents. This approach allows us to construct a semantic relevancy-aware setting that is strictly differentiated from the related information.

Mixed information Mixed information refers to contexts containing both related and unrelated information. In real-world scenarios, considering that queries rarely contain fully related or unrelated information alone, we reconstruct a more challenging setting of mixed context for the model.

We build the context to include an equal proportion of the previously extracted related and unrelated information based on their similarity to the query. From the related information, we sequentially select the top paragraphs with the highest cosine similarity to the query. Conversely, from the unrelated information, we sequentially select the

bottom paragraphs with the lowest similarity to the query. This approach enables us to verify whether the model can provide accurate responses by effectively filtering the task-relevant information within semantically mixed contexts.

Figure 3 illustrates an example of the mixed context from our proposed data construction method. The original example includes a document titled "Jingle Bell Rock," a question-answer pair, and the ground truth (GT) paragraph supporting the answer. The related information comprises paragraphs highly relevant to the query. Consequently, within the same document titled "Jingle Bell Rock," highly relevant paragraphs are selected. In contrast, the unrelated information consists of the least relevant paragraphs from the least relevant document. Therefore, text from an unrelated document titled "Steam" is selected. This mixed composition approach is useful for evaluating whether the model can clearly distinguish between relevant and irrelevant information.

Additionally, we employ ROUGE-L (Lin, 2004), based on n-gram matching with the reference, to measure the similarity between the generated answers and the reference answers. We also utilize the Exact Match (EM) score as supplementary indicator to assess the accuracy of generated answers.

# 3.4.2 Evidence Selection Task

To evaluate the preciseness of selecting evidence paragraphs corresponding to answers to queries, we use Accuracy $(\%)$ . We extract evidence numbers from model-generated responses and compare them with GT evidence paragraph numbers.

In preliminary experiments, we observed instances where LLMs did not respond to the evidence selection task. Therefore, we also measure the rate of when the model does not provide an answer to the instruction (no answer). If the generated response does not include an evidence number, it is considered a 'no answer' case.

# 4 Experiments and Analysis

In this section, we analyze the results of experimenting with LLMs by feeding challenging contexts that are semantically and structurally diversified in Section 3.2. Additionally, we provide various qualitative analyses (refer to Appendix B).

# 4.1 How Do Context Changes in Semantic and Structure Affect LLMs' QA Abilities?

Following previous research on LLMs responses to context (Xu et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024), we verify the answer generation abilities of LLMs through the QA task. Table 1 shows the evaluation results of the QA task. We observe the capabilities of LLMs in terms of semantic and structural changes across various combinations of diverse information types: related (R), unrelated (U), and mixed information (M). Abbreviations such as 'RAR' represent the order of context composition. For example, 'RAR' indicates the sequence 'related-answer-related'.

First, the results concerning position diversity are as follows: When the surrounding contexts are composed only of related information, i.e., RAR, ARR, and RRA, the F1 performance is lower when the answer paragraph is positioned in the middle compared to the other two cases. This result aligns with previous findings that LLMs tend to lose information positioned in the middle of the context (Liu et al., 2023). Similarly, in contexts composed of unrelated and mixed information, the F1 performance is generally lower when the answer paragraph positioned in middle—UAU and MAM—compared to other positions.

Moreover, the results concerning changes in semantic relevancy during context composition are as follows: When the surrounding contexts are composed solely of related information, the performance is highest regardless of the answer paragraph's position compared to contexts with unrelated or mixed information. Conversely, the lowest performance is observed when only unrelated information is provided.

In real-world scenarios, LLMs' ability to clearly present the evidence source amidst confusing information for their generated responses is crucial. Firstly, from a semantic perspective, LLMs achieve the highest accuracy when the surrounding contexts are composed solely of unrelated information. Conversely, the evidence selection ability of LLMs is most diminished when the contexts are composed of related information. Moreover, from a structural perspective, the evidence selection capability of LLMs is observed to be independent of the position of answer paragraphs.

The proportion of 'no answer' responses based on the location of the answer paragraph is in the following order: in the bottom, middle, and top, respectively. In other words, as the answer paragraph is placed later in the context, LLMs' instruction-following ability for the evidence selection task decreases significantly.

# 4.3 Alignment Probing: Do LLMs' QA Capabilities Align with Evidence Selection Abilities?

As seen in the lower box of Figure 2, LLMs may fail to correctly identify the evidence source from the context even if they provide the correct answer. Bridging the misalignment between LLM's abilities across tasks is crucial for preventing hallucinations and ensuring the explainability of LLM's generative behavior. To this end, we explore the task alignment between LLMs' answer generation and evidence selection abilities.

Figure 4 and Figure 5 illustrate the alignment of the QA task and the evidence selection task. The terminology used in the figures is categorized as follows:

- The correctness of answers of LLMs in QA tasks is indicated as either 'Correct' or 'Wrong.'   
- The accuracy of evidence selection of LLMs is indicated as correct $(\mathrm{Acc}^{+})$ , incorrect $(\mathrm{Acc}^{-})$

or no answer $(\mathrm{Acc}^0)$

We find discrepancies in the alignment between QA and evidence selection tasks. In Figure 4, the proportion of cases where both QA and evidence selection tasks are performed correctly (Correct, $\mathrm{Acc}^+$ in red) is comparable to the proportion where QA is incorrect but evidence selection is correct (Wrong, $\mathrm{A

the alignment between QA and evidence selection tasks. In Figure 4, the proportion of cases where both QA and evidence selection tasks are performed correctly (Correct, $\mathrm{Acc}^+$ in red) is comparable to the proportion where QA is incorrect but evidence selection is correct (Wrong, $\mathrm{Acc}^+$ in green). Additionally, the proportion of cases where both QA and evidence selection tasks are performed incorrectly (Wrong, $\mathrm{Acc}^-$ in blue) is low.

This indicates that the LLMs' abilities in the QA task do not necessarily lead to their evidence selection abilities, resulting in the task misalignment phenomenon. Particularly, in Figure 5, the proportion of cases where both QA and evidence selection tasks are incorrect (Wrong, Acc $^{-}$ in blue) is lowest in the unrelated information context compared to the related or mixed information contexts. This suggests that task misalignment is most pronounced in contexts involving unrelated contexts.

Therefore, we provide insight that even when LLMs are given contexts with the same semantic and structural context, performance mismatches between the tasks can occur. For this reason, unrelated information can act as noise and interfere with generation in the QA tasks where the LLMs' ability to synthesize information and evidence is crucial. Conversely, in the evidence selection task, related information can confuse the model when extracting the evidence source.

# 5 Conclusion One of the challenges of utilizing long-context knowledge in real-world scenarios is that the knowledge context does not contain information only helpful for generation. Consequently, LLMs often generate hallucinated contents or fail to adequately present the evidence source for their responses. Therefore, we examine and interpret the phenomenon of discrepancies in LLMs' abilities when performing two different tasks—QA and evidence selection—simultaneously using the same input features, from the perspective of task alignment. To address this, we propose a task alignment verifi

ir responses. Therefore, we examine and interpret the phenomenon of discrepancies in LLMs' abilities when performing two different tasks—QA and evidence selection—simultaneously using the same input features, from the perspective of task alignment. To address this, we propose a task alignment verification framework and resource construction methodology based on the concepts of semantic relevance and structural diversity. Through extensive experiments and analysis in settings that closely resemble real-world scenarios, we provide various insights to bridge the task alignment gap observed in LLMs. We hope our work serves as useful reference material for preventing hallucinations and enhancing the explainability of LLMs' generative behavior when given long contexts.

# Limitations

Despite the significant contributions of this study, there are several limitations that need to be ac

knowledgeed.

First, due to resource constraints, our experiments were limited to only three different LLMs. While these models were selected to provide a diverse representation, a broader range of models could potentially offer more comprehensive insights into task alignment issues. Future work should consider including a wider variety of models to validate and extend the findings of this study.

Second, the constructed contexts in our experiments were designed to reflect realistic scenarios as much as possible, but they still may not capture the full complexity of real-world applications. The dynamics of user interactions and the variety of external knowledge sources in practical settings might present additional challenges not fully addressed by our study. Therefore, real-world testing and validation in diverse application domains would be beneficial to further substantiate our findings.

Finally, while our framework and methodology provide a robust approach to evaluating task alignment, there is room for refinement in terms of measurement granularity and the evaluation metrics used. More nuanced metrics could potentially offer deeper insights into the alignment discrepancies observed between QA and evidence selection tasks.

Despite these limitations, this study offers valuable contributions to understanding the alignment between QA and evidence selection tasks in LLMs, particularly in the context of long and complex external knowledge. Our findings highlight important areas for improvement and provide a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing the reliability and explanatory power of LLM-generated responses in real-world applications.

# Ethics Statement

We discuss the main ethical considerations of the model we proposed: (1) Privacy. the datasets adopted to construct our model provide factual knowledge and fictional person's preferences, and our model does not contain privacy issues. (2) Potential problems. Although we take conscientious steps to ensure the quality of our models, there can still be potential problems with the generated responses' quality,

struct our model provide factual knowledge and fictional person's preferences, and our model does not contain privacy issues. (2) Potential problems. Although we take conscientious steps to ensure the quality of our models, there can still be potential problems with the generated responses' quality, which can lead to incorrect predictions in applications that leverage factual information and human preferences. (3) Model deployment. Our approach employs the Large Language Models (LLMs) for the downstream tasks, which have the risk of reflecting the bias of the training data. It is

a well-known threat in tasks using LLMs, and we should be careful about social impact when using this method since our model aims to handle factual knowledge.
